title: Achieving the limits of automorphism gates
authors: Jin Ming Koh, Shayan Majidy, Aranya Chakraborty, Anqi Gong, Shi Jie Samuel Tan, Norman Y. Yao
abstract: Universal fault-tolerant quantum computing combines versatile but expensive operations with specialized but cheap ones. Its efficiency depends on how much computation can be pushed onto the cheap operations and on the size of the code needed to do so. Automorphism gates provide such cheap operations using only physical single-qubit Clifford gates and qubit permutations. Yet no general theory characterizes their maximum logical power or the minimum code size needed to attain it. We develop such a theory. For stabilizer codes encoding $k\geq3$ logical qubits, we show that the largest logical group attainable by automorphisms is generated by all addressable $S$ and $\mathrm{CX}$ gates, and we construct codes attaining it. While this group contains exponentially fewer gates than the full Clifford group, adding one suitable non-Clifford gate yields universality. We further classify the largest logical groups attainable using qubit permutations, physical single-qubit Cliffords, or both across general stabilizer and CSS codes, and derive refined bounds for self-dual CSS subclasses. Achieving the maximum-size logical group through automorphisms requires $n=Θ(2^k)$ physical qubits. By contrast, all addressable diagonal Clifford gates, generated by $S$ and $\mathrm{CZ}$, require only $n=Θ(k^2)$ physical qubits when implemented using physical single-qubit Cliffords alone. Both bounds are tight. This polynomial qubit cost extends beyond Cliffords to all addressable diagonal gates at any fixed level of the Clifford hierarchy, using physical single-qubit diagonal gates. Thus, for full addressability, the sharpest physical-qubit cost divide lies between diagonal and $\mathrm{CX}$-type gates, not between Clifford and non-Clifford gates.
summary: This paper develops a comprehensive theory characterizing the logical power and resource cost of using automorphism gates in quantum error correction. It shows that while automorphisms can generate large logical groups, the required physical qubit overhead scales exponentially for CX gates but only polynomially for diagonal gates. This establishes a critical resource trade-off for building scalable quantum computers.
main_problem: The paper develops a complete theory to characterize the maximum logical gate group and the minimum physical code size required to achieve it using automorphism gates in fault-tolerant quantum computing.
main_result: The sharpest physical-qubit cost divide for achieving logical gates is between diagonal and CX-type gates, not between Clifford and non-Clifford gates. Furthermore, achieving the maximum automorphism group requires an exponentially large number of physical qubits ($\Theta(2^k)$) compared to diagonal gates ($\Theta(k^2)$).
method: The authors use theoretical group theory, analyzing the structure of logical groups generated by physical single-qubit Clifford gates and qubit permutations within the framework of stabilizer codes.
model_or_system: The study focuses on fault-tolerant quantum computation implemented using stabilizer codes, specifically analyzing general, CSS, and related subclasses of codes encoding $k$ logical qubits.
key_observables: The largest attainable logical gate group, the minimum physical qubit cost ($n$), and the number of logical qubits ($k$).
important_parameters: The number of logical qubits ($k$), the physical qubit cost ($n$), and the type of physical gates used (e.g., single-qubit Cliffords, CX gates).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the code is indecomposable and relies on characterizing the automorphism group $	ext{AutL}(C)$ relative to transversal and permutation logical gates.
figures_summary: Figures summarize the comparison of logical gate implementations and their associated physical-qubit costs for different gate sets (e.g., $\Theta(2k)$ for CX vs. $\Theta(k^2)$ for CZ).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the problem using automorphism gates, then deriving bounds and constructing codes for specific gate sets (S, CX, CZ) across various code classes (CSS, PSD, SSD), culminating in a comparison of the physical cost scaling.
why_interesting: This work provides fundamental theoretical limits on resource overhead in quantum computation, directly impacting the design of fault-tolerant quantum hardware architectures.

(a) Logical gates implemented using physical single-qubit gates and permutations are cheap: they are depth one, require no ancillas, and do not spread errors when the permutations are performed by rearranging qubits or relabelling them in software. (b) For single-qubit Cliffords, permutations, and their combination (automorphisms), we show the largest logical group achievable, a generating gate set, and a code construction attaining it; all maxima are tight. Figure 2. Classes of codes. CSS codes admit separate X- and Z-type stabilizers. We distinguish permutationally self- dual (PSD) codes, whose X- and Z-stabilizer spaces coincide up to a qubit permutation, and strictly self-dual (SSD) codes, for which they coincide directly.

Figure 3. Number of logical gates in each logical group. Solid lines (other than grey) denote tight logical groups for au- tomorphism, transversal, and permutation gates; dotted lines denote additional diagonal logical groups achievable by code constructions at level t of the Clifford hierarchy. We plot the number of logical gates (i.e. order of the logical groups) against the number of logical qubits k in (a) and the mini- mum required number of physical qubits in (b). For scale, markers indicate k = 9 on each curve when the corresponding point lies within the displayed range.

Figure 4. Complete-hypergraph CSS codes. For any t, these codes realize every diagonal logical gate in the tth level of the Clifford hierarchy transversally, through tensor products of single-qubit rotations. The code is defined on the rank-t complete hypergraph of k vertices—with one hyperedge per nonempty subset of ≤t vertices—placing one qubit per hyperedge. Here qubits are labelled by the vertices in the hyperedges omitting set notation (e.g. 12 for {1, 2}). Rows: stabilizers, logical Pauli representatives, and transversal gates (examples highlighted).
